title: How Pinewood Derbies Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the Pinewood Derby, the gravity-powered wooden toy car racing event for Cub Scouts and Boy Scouts. They cover its origin in Manhattan Beach, California in the early 1950s (Don Murphy, inspired by the soapbox derby), the rules (five ounce maximum weight, seven inch length, two and three quarter inch width, three eighths inch rail clearance, no motors or starting devices), design and speed tips (weight distribution toward the rear, baking the wood, straight polished axles, graphite, lighter wheels, rail riding with bent axles, a three-wheel setup), track design, and the problem of parents doing the building. The episode ends with listener mail about a producer's meeting with Alan Alda and a brief tangent on the hosts' own scouting experiences.

segments.title: Opening banter and scouting memories
segments.summary: The hosts plug their social channels and trade stories about their own Cub Scout and Boy Scout experiences, including Chuck quitting after a candy sale and Josh's brother's racing success.

segments.title: What a Pinewood Derby is
segments.summary: Introduction to the Pinewood Derby as a gravity racing event where identical wooden blocks are customized by scouts and parents. The hosts explain potential energy turning to kinetic energy at the start.

segments.title: History: Don Murphy and the first race in 1953
segments.summary: Don Murphy, a Cub Scout leader in Manhattan Beach, California, created the Pinewood Derby as a safer alternative to the soapbox derby for his sons. The first race used standard blocks, wheels and nail axles on a track of about thirty-one feet, with doorbell-based timing. Boys Life Magazine covered it, and the event grew into a national tradition.

segments.title: Official rules and car dimensions
segments.summary: The rules: five ounce maximum weight, seven inch maximum length, two and three quarter inch maximum width, a clearance of three eighths of an inch, and gravity-only propulsion with no motors or starters. Cars ride a central rail. The hosts discuss aerodynamics versus weight and the trade-off between looks and speed.

segments.title: Buying kits, aftermarket parts and legal limits
segments.summary: Kits and aftermarket parts are available, but local leagues set different limits. Some aftermarket wheels appear identical to official ones but have had mass removed. Third-party car building is generally banned.

segments.title: Track design and starting gate
segments.summary: The starting gate is about four feet high and the track runs roughly thirty-two to forty-five feet with two to six lanes. Officials usually place cars. Aluminum tracks like the Micro Wizard system have precise timers, while wooden tracks may require multiple runs per lane to average times.

segments.title: Speed tips: nose shape, weight placement, baking wood, and wheels
segments.summary: Tips from NASA engineer Mark Rober: keep a flat nose, place weight about an inch ahead of the rear axle (around thirty-six percent of speed effect), bake the wood at 250 degrees to remove moisture, and avoid a wheelie. Lighter wheels and a wider wheelbase are also recommended.

segments.title: Axle straightening, rail riding, graphite, and three-wheel cars
segments.summary: Straight, polished axles are checked by spinning them in a drill. Newer advice is rail riding with slightly bent axles so one wheel steers into the rail. Graphite adds about seven percent speed. Lifting one wheel off the track can add speed, but may be illegal in some leagues.

segments.title: Parent involvement, dad divisions and wrap-up
segments.summary: Hosts discuss parents building cars for kids and leagues' responses such as detailed build documentation, dad divisions, and car-building days. They note speeds of about twenty miles per hour that scale to around two hundred miles per hour for a full-sized car. The episode ends with a listener mail about Alan Alda.
